# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–15 (Complete – Updated 118)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: **Autumn of fourth year; Early morning of Waterloo campaign battle day—Regiment receives marching orders; troops march within hours. French crossed Sambre; British left engaged. Bugle signals at dawn; Brussels awakens to drums and pipes. Regiment departs in early morning; sun rising. After departure: Jos remains in Brussels commanding small establishment; Amelia invalided; sun high in heavens; regiment miles on march before Jos appears at breakfast. Afternoon: dinner-hour at half-past two arrives; Jos attempts to coax Amelia to dine; Mrs. O'Dowd joins Jos for meal; wind off water smells of salt and tar; light goes early.**
- **Earlier Timeline**: Spring of fourth year with Seena Orlwood drowned; Winter of third year with frost; Evening at Brighton; Fine moonlight night of May; Army ordered to Belgium; Transports to Ostend; Amelia and Jos to Ramsgate; Belgium in happy season transitioning to war; Famous Brussels ball evening of 15 June 1815 (historical).
- **Primary Locations**: London (Russell Square, Thames Street, Slaughters' hotel, Gray's Inn Square, Hulker and Bullock bankers), Brighton, Mirecombe, Wilhaven, Chatham, Harwich, Fulham, Ramsgate, Ostend, Brussels (Hotel de Ville, Park, Hotel du Parc, opera-house, restaurateur's, Place of Arms), Belgium, Salwick harbor town, Salford, Miremere, Gulton, Salwick.

## Main Characters

**Captain William Dobbin** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- Before departure: Came to Jos's quarters at dawn; roused Jos; instructed him with utmost seriousness to remain in Brussels, watch over Amelia, comfort her, ensure no harm comes to her. Expected personal comfort from final view of Amelia; his selfishness punished. Saw her wrapped in white morning dress, hair falling, large eyes fixed without light, holding George's sash against bosom from which heavy net of crimson dropped like stain of blood. "Good God," thought he, "and is it grief like this I dared to pry into?" Stood powerless and torn with pity. Mind set at ease Jos had committed to conduct toward sister.
- **Deeply troubled by guilt over hastening marriage. Secret adoration of Amelia is his "greatest privilege and hope of life"; privately resolved he would not have let her go to Belgium if married to her. Knows Amelia considers him plain, awkward, ungainly.**
- **Reputation**: "Greatly respected in the regiment, as the best officer and the cleverest man in it."

**George Osborne** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- **Final Departure**: At sound of stirring call to battle, jumped away from gentle arms in which dallying; felt shame at detention. Sun just rising as march began—gallant sight—band led column; George came marching at head of his company. He looked up, smiled at Amelia, and passed on; sound of music died away.
- **Critical Final Hours**: Upon receiving news at play-table, gave wild hurray, clapped glass, walked away speedily. Nerves quivered with excitement; thought about thousand things—past life, future chances, fate, wife, child perhaps unseen. Wished night's work undone and could say farewell to tender and guileless being by whose love he set little store. Thought over brief married life; frightfully dissipated little capital; had been wild and reckless. If mischance befalls him, what left for her? How unworthy he was. Remembered father's generosity. Sat down and wrote farewell letter to father; sealed and kissed superscription; thought how he deserted generous father and thousand kindnesses. **Had looked into Amelia's bedroom; she lay quiet with eyes seemed closed; glad she was asleep. Upon returning, found regimental servant making departure preparations. Debated whether to wake Amelia or leave note for Jos. Went in to look at her once again. She had been awake when he first entered but kept eyes closed so wakefulness should not seem to reproach him. When he returned, her timid heart felt more at ease; she turned towards him, fell into light sleep. George came in and looked again, entering more softly. By pale night-lamp could see her sweet pale face—purple eyelids fringed and closed; one round arm smooth and white lay outside coverlet. He saw how pure, gentle, tender, friendless she was; how selfish, brutal, black with crime he was. Heart-stained and shame-stricken, stood at bed's foot. Came to bedside, looked at little soft hand; bent over pillow noiselessly toward gentle pale face. Two fair arms closed tenderly round his neck as he stooped down. At that moment bugle from Place of Arms began sounding clearly, taken up through town; amidst drums and pipes, whole city awoke; George departed with regiment.**
- **Earlier Status**: Married Amelia late April without father's consent; disinherited (determination "final and irrevocable"). Receives £2,000 in 4 percent annuities and £100/year widow's allowance for Amelia. Lost £140 to Rawdon at cards; obtained £2,000 cheque from Hulker and Bullock bankers. At Chatham: sent Amelia to mother with carte blanche. At Brussels: ashamed of regiment, resolved to exchange; takes wife to nightly jaunts; carrying on "desperate flirtation" with Rebecca; rides with her whenever free; pretends regimental business to Amelia; consigns wife to solitude or Jos's society; passes evenings in Crawleys' company; loses money to Rawdon; flatters himself wife "dying of love for him." Not quite six weeks married.

**Amelia Osborne** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- **After Departure**: **Invalided; remained for hours silent, motionless, and haggard by windows watching last bayonets of column march away. Pauline the cook consoled her; both wept together; each pitied and soothed other. Later, when Rebecca arrived without warning, Rebecca's appearance struck Amelia with terror and made her shrink back; recalled her to world and remembrance of yesterday. In overpowering fears about tomorrow she had forgotten Rebecca—jealousy—everything except that her husband was gone and in danger. Until Rebecca came in and broke the spell, we too had forborne to enter that sad chamber. How long had that poor girl been on her knees! what hours of speechless prayer and bitter prostration had she passed there! After first movement of terror when Rebecca's green eyes lighted upon her, a feeling of anger succeeded; her face flushed red; she returned Rebecca's look with steadiness which surprised and somewhat abashed her rival. Amelia drew back her hand—never since her life began had that gentle soul refused any demonstration of good-will or affection. But she drew back her hand and trembled all over. Asked with solemnity: "Why are you here, Rebecca?" These glances troubled Rebecca. Amelia spoke with spirit and volubility Rebecca had never before seen in her, and before which Rebecca was quite dumb. Accused Rebecca: "When you were quite poor, who was it that befriended you? Was I not a sister to you? You saw us all in happier days before he married me. I was all in all then to him; or would he have given up his fortune, his family, as he nobly did to make me happy? Why did you come between my love and me? Who sent you to separate those whom God joined, and take my darling's heart from me--my own husband? Do you think you could love him as I did? His love was everything to me. You knew it, and wanted to rob me of it. For shame, Rebecca; bad and wicked woman--false friend and false wife." Continued in more pitiful tone: "But what have I done to you, that you should try and take him from me? I had him but for six weeks. You might have spared me those, Rebecca. And yet, from the very first day of our wedding, you came and blighted it. Now he is gone, are you come to see how unhappy I am? You made me wretched enough for the past fortnight: you might have spared me to-day." Then in wilder tone: "No. You didn't come. You took him away. Are you come to fetch him from me? He was here, but he is gone now. There on that very sofa he sate. Don't touch it. We sate and talked there. I was on his knee, and my arms were round his neck, and we said 'Our Father.' Yes, he was here: and they came and took him away, but he promised me to come back." Showed Rebecca George's sash: "Look, this is his sash--isn't it a pretty colour?" Took up fringe and kissed it; had tied it round her waist. Forgot her anger, her jealousy, very presence of rival seemingly. Walked silently and almost with smile toward bed, began to smooth down George's pillow. Refused Jos's invitation to dine, saying "You are very good and kind, Joseph...but, if you please, I will stay in my room to-day." Later, presence of Mrs. O'Dowd (more resolute friend) checked Amelia's weakness; she was better of this control and company. Hearts with column as it marched farther away. Dreadful doubt and anguish—prayers and fears and griefs unspeakable—followed the regiment. It was the women's tribute to the war.**
- **Earlier Status**: Troubled by Rebecca's wit and misgivings about her. Not quite six weeks married. Aware George carrying on flirtation with Rebecca; does not plague him with jealousy but becomes unhappy and pines miserably in secret. At Brussels ball: did not know soul; sat unnoticed in corner except when Dobbin brought refreshments. Witnessing Rebecca's request for George's scarf and flowers proved "quite too much for her"; clung to Dobbin, called him by Christian name, begged him to take her home; did not sleep that night.

**Captain Rawdon Crawley** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- **Departure**: At sound of stirring call to battle, same feeling of eagerness and excitement amongst friends. Upon receiving final news campaign opened and troops to march, gravity became such that Rebecca rallied him, which hurt his feelings. Said with tremor: "You don't suppose I'm afraid, Becky, I should think. But I'm a pretty good mark for a shot, and you see if it brings me down, why I leave one and perhaps two behind me whom I should wish to provide for, as I brought 'em into the scrape. It is no laughing matter that, Mrs. C., anyways." This showed genuine concern—previously had seldom thought about anything but himself until last few months when Love obtained mastery over dragoon. Made last dispositions: went through various items of little catalogue of effects, striving to see how they might be turned into money for Rebecca's benefit in case any accident befall him. Dressed himself in oldest and shabbiest uniform and epaulets, leaving newest behind under wife's (or widow's) guardianship. This famous dandy went off on campaign with kit as modest as that of sergeant, and with something like prayer on his lips for woman he was leaving. Took her up from ground, held her in his arms for minute, tight pressed against strong-beating heart. Face was purple and eyes dim as he put her down and left her. Rode by his General's side, smoked cigar in silence as they hastened after troops; not until some miles on their way that he left off twirling moustache and broke silence.
- **Earlier Status**: Secretly married to Rebecca; heavily indebted. In Brussels: lodging at Hotel du Parc with Rebecca and General Tufto. Repeatedly together with George now; George always welcome in quarters.

**Rebecca Sharp (Mrs. Rebecca Rawdon Crawley)** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- **Post-Departure Actions**: **Wisely determined not to give way to unavailing sentimentality on Rawdon's departure. Waved him adieu from window; stood moment looking after he was gone. Cathedral towers and full gables of quaint old houses just beginning to blush in sunrise. Had been no rest for her that night. Still in pretty ball-dress, fair hair hanging somewhat out of curl, circles round eyes dark with watching. Put bouquet of ball into glass of water and went to bed and slept very comfortably. Found in Rawdon's pocket-book draft for twenty pounds on Osborne's banker; determined to get it cashed and pay visit afterwards to "poor little Emmy." Made calculations of Rawdon's valuables; found with pungent feeling of triumph and self-satisfaction that should circumstances occur, she might reckon on six or seven hundred pounds at very least, to begin world with. Passed morning disposing, ordering, looking out, and locking up her properties in most agreeable manner. After visiting Jos (whom she flattered and manipulated into emotional state with false sympathy and strategically placed remarks), Rebecca went to comfort Amelia. Visited Amelia without warning; greeted her with extended arms to embrace her. Rebecca of good-natured and obliging disposition; liked Amelia rather than otherwise. Even Amelia's hard words, reproachful as they were, were complimentary—groans of person stinging under defeat. Meeting Mrs. O'Dowd afterwards in Park, Rebecca accosted the latter to her surprise, informing her that poor little Mrs. Osborne was in desperate condition and almost mad with grief, sent off good-natured Irishwoman straight to see if she could console her young favourite. Mrs. O'Dowd replied: "I've cares of my own enough...But if she's so bad as you say, and you can't attend to her, who used to be so fond of her, faith I'll see if I can be of service." Rebecca watched her marching off with smile on lip. Had keenest sense of humour; Parthian look which retreating Mrs. O'Dowd flung over her shoulder almost upset Mrs. Crawley's gravity. Becky thought: "My service to ye, me fine Madam, and I'm glad to see ye so cheerful...It's not YOU that will cry your eyes out with grief, anyway."**
- **Earlier Status**: Secretly married to Rawdon; heavily indebted. Packed chief valuables sent to London. In Belgium: lodging at Hotel du Parc with Rawdon and General Tufto. At opera: performed hand-kissing toward Amelia's box; clapped hands when George entered her box. Rebecca remarked to George: thought Amelia jealous at Brighton; now supposes scandalized because Rawdon, Rebecca, and General live together. Invited George to dinner; General dines with Commander-in-Chief. At Brussels ball: invited; danced with George twice or thrice; made request to George for scarf and flowers (done twenty times before in last few days).

**Jos Sedley** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- **Current Status After Departure**: Left in command of little colony at Brussels with Amelia invalided, Isidor (Belgian servant), and bonne (maid-of-all-work) as garrison. Rest broken by sounding of bugles in early morning. Though disturbed in spirit, nevertheless remained for many hours in bed, wakeful and rolling about until usual hour of rising arrived. Sun high in heavens and regiment miles on their march before civilian appeared in flowered dressing-gown at breakfast. Amelia could not come to breakfast; her bonne said Madame great deal too ill and had been in frightful state ever since husband's departure. Jos showed his sympathy by pouring her out large cup of tea; improved on this; not only sent her breakfast, but bethought him what delicacies she would most like for dinner. After Rebecca's visit inflamed his heart with emotional investment, Jos remains conflicted—thoughts glowing maddening upon contemplation of enchanting Rebecca; anon shrinking guiltily before vision of jealous Rawdon Crawley with his curling, fierce mustachios and terrible duelling pistols loaded and cocked. At half-past two, dinner-hour arrived. Warriors may fight and perish, but he must dine. He came into Amelia's room to see if he could coax her to share that meal. "Try," said he; "the soup is very good. Do try, Emmy," and he kissed her hand. Except when she was married, he had not done so much for years before. Amelia declined, preferring to stay in her room.
- **Earlier Status**: Profoundly mortified by Rebecca's inattention during Brussels stay; never presented to Rawdon Crawley's great acquaintances; scarcely invited to her parties; too timid to play much; his presence bored George and Rawdon equally. But Rebecca's words and knowing tender glances inflamed his heart; all doubts and suspicions forgotten.

**Mrs. Major Peggy O'Dowd** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- **After Departure**: **Upon understanding regiment will march next morning, became very grave. After regiment's departure, betook herself to large volume of uncle the Dean's sermons for meditation; perhaps did not understand much; thoughts were elsewhere; sleep project with poor Mick's nightcap on pillow was quite vain one. She who remains and suffers—has leisure to think, brood, remember. Wandering very disconsolately in Park following morning, was accosted by Rebecca, who informed her that poor little Mrs. Osborne was in desperate condition and almost mad with grief. Mrs. O'Dowd replied: "I've cares of my own enough...But if she's so bad as you say, and you can't attend to her, who used to be so fond of her, faith I'll see if I can be of service." Speedily found way to Mrs. Osborne's lodgings. Found Amelia still at bedside, standing almost crazy with grief. The Major's wife, a stronger-minded woman, endeavoured her best to comfort her young friend. "You must bear up, Amelia, dear," she said kindly, "for he mustn't find you ill when he sends for you after the victory. It's not you are the only woman that are in the hands of God this day." Amelia replied: "I know that. I am very wicked, very weak." Presence of more resolute friend checked Amelia's weakness; she was better of this control and company. They went on till two o'clock; their hearts were with column as it marched farther and farther away. Dreadful doubt and anguish—prayers and fears and griefs unspeakable—followed the regiment. It was the women's tribute to the war. It taxes both alike, and takes the blood of the men, and the tears of the women. At half-past two, Jos came to invite her to dine. The soup was very good. The savour of the soup was agreeable to Mrs. O'Dowd's nostrils: and she thought she would bear Mr. Jos company. So the two sate down to their meal. "God bless the meat," said the Major's wife, solemnly: she was thinking of her honest Mick, riding at the head of his regiment: "'Tis but a bad dinner those poor boys will get to-day," she said, with a sigh, and then, like a philosopher, fell to.**
- **Major Mick O'Dowd**: Most modest, silent, sheep-faced, meek of little men; obedient to wife. Upon understanding regiment will march next morning, placidly pulled nightcap over his ears, told Peggy there would be such a ball danced in a day or two as some of 'em had never heard the chune of; much more happy to retire to rest. Asked to be woken half an hour before assembly beats, called at half-past one, things ready; may be he'll not come back to breakfast; words signified opinion that regiment would march next morning.

**Isidor (Belgian Servant)** [MINOR CHARACTER]
- **Current Attitude and Intelligence**: Looked on very sulkily while Osborne's servant disposed of master's baggage previous to Captain's departure. In first place hated Mr. Osborne, whose conduct to him and inferiors was generally overbearing; secondly, angry that so many valuables should be removed from under his hands, to fall into other people's possession when English discomfiture should arrive. Of this defeat he and vast number of other persons in Brussels and Belgium did not make slightest doubt. Almost universal belief was that Emperor would divide Prussian and English armies, annihilate one after other, and march into Brussels before three days were over: when all movables of present masters, who would be killed, or fugitives, or prisoners, would lawfully become property of Monsieur Isidor. Became self-declared partisan of Napoleon; took proclamation from his pocket and sternly thrust it into Jos's face; already looked upon frogged coat and valuables as his own spoil. Said: "The Prussians were three to one at Jena, and he took their army and kingdom in a week. They were six to one at Montmirail, and he scattered them like sheep. The Austrian army is coming, but with the Empress and the King of Rome at its head; and the Russians, bah! the Russians will withdraw. No quarter is to be given to the English, on account of their cruelty to our braves on board the infamous pontoons. Look here, here it is in black and white. Here's the proclamation of his Majesty the Emperor and King." Informed Jos: "His papers are burned, his effects are removed, and his quarters are being got ready for the Duke of Dalmatia."

**Pauline (Cook)** [MINOR CHARACTER]
- Amelia's attendant. Much less selfishly disposed than Isidor. Few dependents could come near Amelia, kind and gentle creature, without paying usual tribute of loyalty and affection to her sweet and affectionate nature. When found Amelia remained for hours silent, motionless, and haggard by windows watching last bayonets of column march away, honest girl took lady's hand and said Pauline's own man was also in the army; burst into tears; Amelia falling into her arms did likewise; each pitied and soothed other.

**John Osborne (Old Mr. Osborne)** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- Wealthy merchant; George's father; savage, determined man. Upon learning George married Amelia, erupted in fury. George ceases to be family member. News how son is entertaining peers and peeresses came to Osborne's ears in the City. George wrote farewell letter to him at dawn before regiment's departure, remembering his past generosity and thousand kindnesses, sealed and kissed superscription.

**General Tufto** [MINOR CHARACTER]
- Military officer in Brussels with considerable status. Lodging at Hotel du Parc with Rawdon and Rebecca. Dines out almost constantly. At opera: disengaged eye working round in Rebecca's direction, shooting out bloodshot glances at her and George. When Rebecca left box with George, gave low utterance to curses "so deep, that no compositor would venture to print them." Was jealous and angry; capable of generating such lust and fury, rage and hatred.

## Critical Facts and Status

**WATERLOO CAMPAIGN - BATTLE COMMENCED AND REGIMENT DEPARTED**: French have crossed Sambre; British left already engaged. **Regiment now miles on their march; Jos left in command of Brussels establishment with Amelia invalided, Isidor, and bonne as garrison under him. Afternoon arrives with dinner-hour at half-past two.**

**GEORGE-AMELIA MARRIAGE - SEVERED AT CRITICAL MOMENT**: Married late April; disinherited "final and irrevocable"; receives £2,000 in 4 percent annuities and £100/year widow's allowance for Amelia. Not quite six weeks married. **At final moment before departure: George bent over Amelia's bedside; she awoke and threw her fair arms round his neck with sob; at that moment bugle from Place of Arms began sounding clearly, taken up through town; amidst drums and pipes, whole city awoke; George departed with regiment. After departure: Amelia invalided; remained for hours silent, motionless, and haggard by windows watching last bayonets of column march away; Pauline the cook consoled her; both wept together; each pitied and soothed other.**

**REBECCA'S CUNNING AND MANIPULATION - CONSOLIDATES POSITION**: Upon Rawdon's departure, wisely determined not to give way to sentimentality. **After visiting Jos (whom she flattered and manipulated), Rebecca went to comfort Amelia, securing Jos's continued emotional investment and establishing secure retreat with him. Rebecca's calculation: "If the worst comes to the worst, my retreat is secure; and I have a right-hand seat in the barouche." After visiting Amelia, Rebecca met Mrs. O'Dowd and successfully directed her to Amelia's bedside, positioning herself as concerned friend while Mrs. O'Dowd provides solace. Rebecca of good-natured and obliging disposition; liked Amelia rather than otherwise. However, Rebecca's role in George's flirtation and emotional distance from Amelia now exposed—Amelia voiced her accusations with volubility and spirit Rebecca had never before seen in her, and before which Rebecca was quite dumb.**

**BELGIAN AND BRUSSELS STAFF ASSESSMENTS - INTENSIFIES COLLAPSE FEARS**: Isidor and vast number of other persons in Brussels and Belgium did not make slightest doubt of English discomfiture. Almost universal belief was that Emperor would divide Prussian and English armies, annihilate one after other, and march into Brussels before three days were over. Jos knows nothing of what passing in servants' minds; they marking him down for plunder when English are defeated. **Isidor now openly declares himself partisan of Napoleon; believes Belgian nobility fleeing (Duchess, Duc de Richemont) confirm inevitable French victory. Afternoon light goes early as wind comes off water with smell of salt and tar.**

**WOMEN'S SUFFERING DURING CAMPAIGN - ESTABLISHED AS CENTRAL THEME**: War chroniclers who write brilliant stories of fight and triumph scarcely tell of women's hours of speechless prayer and bitter prostration. These are too mean parts of pageant; you don't hear widows' cries or mothers' sobs in midst of shouts and jubilation in great Chorus of Victory. Yet when was time that such have not cried out: heart-broken, humble protestants, unheard in uproar of triumph? It was the women's tribute to the war. It taxes both alike, and takes the blood of the men, and the tears of the women.
